Bayesian Discount Prior: Comparison Between Current and Historical Data

Source: R/probability_discount.R
probability_discount.Rd

An educational calculation of the current-historical comparison for normal summary data. This helper is not used internally. The fixed method returns twice the smaller directional posterior probability; the Monte Carlo method returns a normal-tail comparison for each draw.

Usage

probability_discount(
  mu = NULL,
  sigma = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  mu0 = NULL,
  sigma0 = NULL,
  N0 = NULL,
  number_mcmc = 10000,
  method = "fixed"
)

Arguments

mu

scalar. Mean of the current data.

sigma

scalar. Standard deviation of the current data.

N

scalar. Number of observations of the current data.

mu0

scalar. Mean of the historical data.

sigma0

scalar. Standard deviation of the historical data.

N0

scalar. Number of observations of the historical data.

number_mcmc

scalar. Number of Monte Carlo simulations. Default is 10000.

method

character. Default "fixed" estimates a directional probability q and returns 2 * min(q, 1 - q). With "mc", each pair of mean draws is standardized by its conditional standard error and converted to a two-sided normal-tail comparison. See the normal vignette for details.

Value

A numeric comparison in [0, 1]: one value under "fixed", or a vector of length number_mcmc under "mc".

Details

This is a borrowing comparison, not a posterior probability of equality or equivalence. Weight variation under "mc" is part of that procedure; more draws improve the precision of its distributional summaries. The baseline prior for each source is proportional to \(1 / \sigma^2\). The fixed method uses direct Monte Carlo simulation.

References

Haddad, T., Himes, A., Thompson, L., Irony, T., Nair, R. MDIC Computer Modeling and Simulation working group.(2017) Incorporation of stochastic engineering models as prior information in Bayesian medical device trials. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 1-15.

Examples

probability_discount(
  mu = 0, sigma = 1, N = 100,
  mu0 = 0.1, sigma0 = 1, N0 = 100
)
#> [1] 0.4922
